title: The End of the DST: What Happens When Your Client's Hold Period Is Over
summary: DSTs are built to sell. Learn the three exit paths at the end of a DST hold period: taking the cash, a new 1031 exchange, or a 721 UPREIT, and how advisors can prepare clients.
body_markdown:
Advisors spend most of their 1031 energy on the front end of a DST: identification deadlines, sponsor diligence, lease terms. Less attention goes to the back end. But your client will eventually ask the obvious question: how does this end? Having a clean answer is what separates a transaction broker from a trusted advisor.


Every DST is built around a defined life. The IRS framework that makes DSTs work for 1031 exchanges (Revenue Ruling 2004-86) requires the trust to hold the property for its life and then dispose of it, typically in five to ten years depending on the offering. A DST is not a permanent holding vehicle. From day one, the plan is to sell.


When that day comes, your client generally faces three paths.


Path one: take the cash. The trustee sells the property, pays off any obligations, and distributes the net proceeds to beneficiaries pro rata. This is the simplest exit, and it is taxable. The deferral ends, and the capital gains and depreciation recapture your client deferred on the way in come due. For some clients that is exactly right. A retiring owner who wants liquidity, or an estate that prefers cash to property, may welcome the exit. Just make sure the client understands the tax bill is coming, and that it includes everything deferred from prior exchanges, not just this one.


Path two: exchange again. Nothing in the rules says the 1031 journey has to end with the DST. The proceeds from a DST sale can roll into a new 1031 exchange, with the same 45-day identification and 180-day closing clocks starting over. For clients who still want deferral, the most common move is into another DST or another like-kind property. This is one reason advisors keep a pipeline of available offerings in view: your client cannot identify replacement property on day 45 if you have not already done the homework.


Path three: the 721 option. Some sponsors offer a conversion into an operating partnership (UPREIT) at the end of the hold period. This converts the client's DST interest into operating partnership units on a tax-deferred basis, which can offer longer-term income and a path to liquidity through share conversion down the road. Availability and terms vary widely by sponsor, and the details live in the PPM, not in a brochure.


There is also the unplanned exit. If a loan defaults or a master tenant fails, some DSTs include a "springing LLC" provision: the trust converts into a limited liability company so the manager can act to protect the property. This is a safety valve, not a strategy. Mention it to show clients you understand the full risk picture.


What should you actually do with this? Three things.


First, read the disposition section of the PPM before your client asks. It describes the stated hold period, how the sale will be marketed, and whether a 721 option exists. If the PPM is vague about the exit, that is a data point.


Second, ask the sponsor directly: what is the plan at year seven? Sponsors that have done this before will answer in specifics. Sponsors that have not will answer in generalities.


Third, set expectations early. Tell the client at entry that the DST has a shelf life and that you will revisit the exit question together a year or two before the projected sale. Nobody wants to hear about the tax bill for the first time in the month it arrives.


Your clients chose you because you think in full cycles. The entry gets the signature. The exit plan earns the relationship.
